description: We’re a team of friends from Kazakhstan passionate about space, technology, and solving real-world problems with data. Our skills cover programming, design, and research, and we’re excited to build something meaningful with NASA’s open data. Our team is already formed, we’re just adding our members here.
summary:
To the Far Side is a single player mission design game built in Godot. The player directs a crewed Moon programme from the Government’s request to the final mission report, across eleven stages: funding trajectory analysis, choosing a landing site and instruments, designing the rocket and spacecraft part by part, picking a launch site, planning operations, and flying the mission.
Every decision is constrained by one shared budget, by mass, power and communications, and by a fixed deadline. The game does not say which choice is right. 
Consequences appear later: at Board reviews, during the build, on launch day or at the Moon. The final report traces each result back to the decision that caused it and compares the flight with a real mission.
The game is grounded in NASA resources: mission segments and project phases, JPL’s Concept Maturity Levels, real launch sites and Apollo landing sites. Its flight path was checked against a lunar transfer computed in NASA’s GMAT.
It matters because mission design is usually taught one topic at a time. Here a beginner can see how the pieces depend on each other, and why real missions succeed or fail.
details:
What it does:

To the Far Side puts the player in the chair of a programme director. The Government wants a crew on the Moon, launched by 20 July 2033, for USD 60 billion. The game starts on 14 November 2026 and runs through 11 stages, from the first request to the final mission report.

The stages follow NASA's real project life cycle, from Pre Phase A to Phase C/D. 

Four gate reviews carry their real names: Mission Concept Review, System Requirements Review, Critical Design Review and Flight Readiness Review. At the gates the Board shows the JPL Concept Maturity Level the project has reached.

How it works:

Flight dynamics. The player decides how much to pay for trajectory work. The team's report explains the free return path, a speed (delta v) budget for six burns, the rocket equation and a Monte Carlo run of 1,000 simulated flights. Less money means a less certain path.

Science plan. Six real Apollo landing sites with their real coordinates, and 11 instruments limited by mass, power and cost. Richer science means a harder landing.

Vehicle. 14 sections and 52 options: stages, lander, capsule, escape system, life support, launch pad, test programme. Apollo style and Artemis style vehicles can both be built, and a live check shows speed, mass, cost and build time.

Launch site. Five real U.S. sites. Latitude and allowed launch directions decide how much of the Earth's spin the rocket keeps: 409 m/s at Kennedy, 240 m/s at Kodiak. Each site has its own weather risk.

Operations. Crew training, mission control, launch team, recovery forces, a single, backup or voting flight computer, and the size of the reserve.

Flight. Ten phases from countdown to splashdown. The player can drop the stages and fly the last 150 metres of the landing by hand. There are seven endings, from a landing to a launch abort.

Mission report. Ten sections: plan against actual, where the money went, and which decision caused each result. It sorts the flight into NASA's four segments (launch, space, ground, user) and names the closest real mission, from Apollo 7 to Artemis II.

The game never says which choice is right. A test skipped in 2027 can end the flight in 2032.

Scientific accuracy:

The flight path is integrated from the gravity of the Earth and the Moon. We compared it with a lunar transfer computed in NASA's GMAT and published in Mission Viz. After four days of coasting the two differ by about 2,700 km, 0.7% of the distance to the Moon.

With the Sun's gravity added, the difference falls to about 3 km. The game shows both numbers to the player.

Landing sites use NSSDCA coordinates, launch sites use Launch Services Program data, and the speed budget follows Apollo 11.

An automated test flies 108 model missions through every ending.

Benefits and impact:

Players learn by doing why missions take years, cost billions and need reviews, reserves and test flights. Terms are explained in plain English, with "Read more" pages and a glossary, so no technical background is needed.

The game runs offline and can be replayed: change one decision, fly again and compare the two reports. It is made for students, teachers and anyone curious about spaceflight.

Tools:

Godot Engine 4.7 with GDScript

Open fonts (Saira, IBM Plex) and map outlines from the U.S. Census Bureau and Natural Earth

NASA open resources: JPL Concept Maturity Levels, Goddard Mission Design Lab, GMAT, Mission Viz, NSSDCA Apollo data, Launch Services Program launch sites

An AI assistant (Claude) helped write the code and produce the art under the team's full direction

Developed on a Mac, exported as one Windows executable

Creativity:

The right answer is hidden, as in real programmes. The player learns what a decision meant only when the flight shows it.

Lessons arrive as in-world documents: an analysis report, board reviews and a mission report, not tutorials.

Every flight ends with "a real mission like yours", which links the player's result to history.

Factors we considered:

Accuracy against simplicity: we left out the Sun's gravity and tell the player what that costs.

Respect: no real people are named, and the game is labelled as fan made, with no NASA logos.

Scope: one mission in depth, not many in brief.
